Objective study: can PCBO follow the simulator’s landscape on its own?

Mug and spoon, μ = 0.6, 10 000 particles, seed 11 unless stated, 11 and 12 November 2026. Requested on 11 November at 17:20: a multi-stage study of how to get a better objective from the simulator’s output. Full account with every number and script: code/results/mug_spoon/r363/objective_study/REPORT.md. Study arms are diagnostics; none is adopted as the solver.

Short answer

The simulator’s output is informative; two things hid it. The earlier runs weighted particles with the fourth root of the cost, which squeezes the whole landscape into a factor of 1.5, and they searched in the coordinates of a settling chart, where the chart has already used up the slope and leaves PCBO a flat floor with cliffs.

If instead each body is only lowered until it first touches something (no settling, no sliding, 0.04 s per update), no scene of the starting population is at rest, and PCBO with the published weights brings 93 % of the particles to rest by itself, in about 4 s per update. Six of the 9337 final scenes had a starting scene within 1 cm, so the scenes are reached by the updates and are not in the starting sample. On two seeds 8503 and 9171 consensus points stay static for 10 s (the earlier solver with its settling chart: 8719).

What the joint search does not reach is a rare placement of one body on a mug that is not yet at rest, such as the spoon inside the upright mug: 84 starting particles have the mug within 1 cm of rest, 81 the spoon, 2 both. In a probe where the mug is given at rest and PCBO places only the spoon, that family is found on seed 11 (93 scenes, all static for 10 s), and over four mug postures the probe holds 19 families with static scenes, as many as the earlier solver with its settling chart. On seed 12 the same probe misses that family (section 9).

1. What the landscape looks like

Each card is one scene at rest and one two-dimensional slice through it, drawn as a surface: the two horizontal directions are two ways of moving the scene, the height is the cost of the moved scene. The scene itself is the green dot at the centre. The same grid of 81 × 81 moved scenes is released for each of the four pictures. Pose coordinates: the moved bodies are released where they are, hovering or overlapping. Touching coordinates: after the move each body is lowered or raised until it just touches what is below it, then released.

at rest (cost 0)

Reading: the first picture of each card is a high plateau with a narrow pit at the scene; that is the landscape you saw. The second is the same cost without the root: walls of overlap penalty wherever a rotation pushes a body into the table or the other body. In touching coordinates (third picture) the surface is a bowl that falls towards the scene over centimetres and tens of degrees, with steps where the spoon loses its support and falls. After 0.2 s instead of 1 s (fourth picture) most of those steps are ramps, because the spoon has not yet fallen far.

2. PCBO without a settling chart

All four runs start from the same 10 000 random poses, none at rest, and use the unchanged update with the published consensus weights. “Reach” is how far a particle looks for a better one: narrow = as far as its own scene moves when released; wide = the paper’s setting with θ > 0.

In pose coordinates the cost of a hovering scene is its fall height, so early on every particle follows the lowest particle within decimetres and 95 % of the population ends with the mug on its side. In touching coordinates there is no fall and the upright and upside-down mugs keep their particles. With the narrow reach two thirds of the particles then stall, each the best within its own reach with nobody to follow; the wide reach removes that.

3. Outcomes

Static 10 s: every consensus point released for 10 s at a 2 ms and at a 1 ms time step; counted when no point of either body moves more than 1 mm in both. Arm S is the earlier fast solver, whose chart settles every scene (two passes per update); it starts with thousands of scenes at rest. Times are per update on a machine shared with a second run; arm Q3 alone on the machine takes 3.8 to 4.3 s per update with all 10 000 particles released (lowering 0.04 s, simulation 3.4 s, consensus 0.4 s).

4. Families

Consensus points at rest in the 1 s release, by the galleries’ contact-based family names (coarse descriptions, not proved components). Where a 10 s check exists the cell reads “static 10 s / at rest 1 s”.

7. What changed the outcome, and what did not

  • The dead zone. The present cost is exactly 0 inside the 1 mm tolerance, so particles stop where they cross it: arm Q’s scenes move 0.8 mm in their release and a fifth creep out within 10 s. Without the dead zone (arm Q3) they move 0.17 mm, and 8503 instead of 6665 stay static.
  • The reach. Narrow: two thirds of the particles stall. Middle (0.1 m): 12 coarse families instead of 9, but 5575 at rest and 1818 stalled. Wide: 9337 at rest.
  • The horizon. Scoring with the first 0.2 s removes most cliffs and takes a third less time, but it favours scenes that start to move slowly: the upright mug loses its particles and the tilted mug gains them. Different families, not more.
  • The level of the bodies. With a level coordinate (arms Q to Q3) the particles that start below the top level are gone after five updates. Without it, every body on its lowest free position (arm Q4), the run reaches the spoon inside the mug lying on its side (87 static scenes) and as many static scenes overall (8600).

8. Why the spoon inside the upright mug is not reached, and a probe that reaches it

Mug within 3 cm / spoon within 3 cm / both538 / 728 / 41

The two excursions are independent (rank correlation 0.04), so the share of particles with both bodies nearly right is the product of the two shares. A particle whose spoon is well placed almost always has a mug that still rolls or tips; it then follows a particle that is better overall and gives up its spoon placement. The simulator returns the excursion of each body separately; the cost adds them and loses which body is wrong.

Probe (arm Q5). One body is given at rest and PCBO places only the other: the mug’s pose is taken from a static scene of arm Q3 (the run’s own result, standing for the stable input scene that is always available), and the search runs over the spoon’s offset and rotation, five numbers. The update, weights, objective and lowering step are unchanged; the objective still charges the spoon for disturbing the mug.

This is a probe for one given mug at a time. It shows that the missing families are reachable once the search is over one body; it is not a method for the joint problem, and scenes in which the mug is held by the spoon are outside it. Correction of 12 November: on seed 12 the probe with the upright mug ends with no spoon inside the mug; on seed 11 the family grew from a single particle that was at rest at the start (section 9). The probes start with 1 to 4 spoons already at rest. The upside-down mug was run with 2000 particles: with all 10 000 mugs resting on their rims the releases take 32 s per update.

9. One body at a time: is it complete, and can a change of coordinates do the same inside one joint run?

Asked on 12 November: whether placing one body at a time would work for a complex scene and is even complete, and whether a mild change of coordinates could make the landscape better behaved on the difficult families. Five measurements, all on the mug and the spoon; nothing here was run on more than two bodies.

9.1 Which known static scenes can be built one body at a time

A scene can be built one body at a time, every intermediate scene at rest, exactly when one of its bodies stays at rest at its pose with the other body taken away. Every consensus scene that is static for 10 s, from all runs that have a 10 s check, was tested that way: each body released alone for 1 s.

9.2 Why the joint search misses the spoon inside the upright mug

In the joint search the spoon has stopped exploring before the mug stands still, so a spoon is never tried on a mug that is at rest. With the mug given at rest the family was found on seed 11, but from very few particles: of the 97 spoons that start inside the mug only one is at rest, and the others gather round it and round a few more that come to rest in the first twenty updates. On seed 12 none of the 74 spoons that start inside is at rest, and in the present coordinates none ends there. In polar coordinates (9.4) the same starting scenes end with 61.

9.3 The landscape around the difficult family

The scene at the green dot is a spoon leaning across the inside of the upright mug, static for 10 s (from the probe). Each card moves it along two coordinates, puts every body on its lowest free position and releases it. First picture: the objective. Second: how far the spoon’s centre of mass descends. Third: 1 where the release ends with the spoon inside the mug.

9.4 Two changes of coordinates, tested

The first body at rest by its own release. Each particle lands its bodies in its own order. The first one is now released alone on the table for 1 s and takes the rotation it ends with; the second is lowered onto it as before. PCBO, weights, objective and lowering step are unchanged, and all coordinates of both bodies are still searched in one run. In the control, the first body only starts at rest and is then free.

Polar coordinates about the first body. The spoon’s position is given by its distance from the mug and the direction round it, and its rotation is taken relative to that direction. The update is applied to these numbers instead of x, y and the rotation in the table frame. The scenes, the objective and the starting scenes are the same.

Families: static 10 s / at rest 1 s. “Probe” columns have the mug given upright and identical starting scenes; they differ only in the coordinates the update acts on.

10. Exploring without being drawn into other valleys

Asked on 12 November, after section 9: the goal is one formulation that finds all families, and “by chance” really means that particles did not explore long enough before being drawn into other valleys. This section measures that and changes the objective and the distance measure accordingly. Everything is still a diagnostic arm. The formulation the section arrives at is written up on its own page, with its definitions, its landscape and a gallery by family: the most successful formulation so far.

10.1 Who follows whom

For every particle with the spoon inside the upright mug that is not yet at rest (updates 0 to 30 of three earlier runs): where is the particle it follows?

10.2 Objective and distance taken from the end of the release

The simulator returns where each scene has got to after its 1 s release. Two changes use that, at no extra cost:

  • Objective: how far the release takes the scene, measured exactly as the distance between scenes is measured (root mean square displacement of the surface points), instead of the largest excursion of any point.
  • Distance between two particles: the distance between their scenes and the distance between the scenes their releases end in, taken together. Two particles are neighbours only if they start near each other and end near each other.

With these, a particle inside the mug sees a scene resting on the rim as far away (its release ends somewhere else), and other particles inside the mug as near. Two settings go with it: the middle reach (0.1 m), and the noise term of the earlier model that keeps a particle moving while its consensus point is not at rest, applied per body.

The same slices as in 9.3, drawn for both objectives on one scale.

10.3 Mug given at rest, seed 12: the case that failed

All runs start from the same 10 000 scenes (74 spoons inside the mug, none at rest) and use the present coordinates. “Stalled” = the particle is its own consensus point and not at rest. Without the noise term stalled particles never move again.

10.5 Which families survive a disturbance

Asked on 12 November: are the families that are never found even strongly stable? Up to 60 static scenes of each family (from all runs) were disturbed four times at each size: both bodies turned by the angle about a random axis and shifted by as many millimetres, put back down, and released for 10 s. A finite numerical test, not a proof.

10.6 The same formulation with no body treated specially

Asked on 12 November: starting one body at rest and measuring the other about it may work for two bodies and not scale. In the joint runs above no body is fixed, but two things are tied to a pair of bodies: the body put down first starts at rest, and the polar coordinates are taken about the mug. A control run drops both (both bodies start with random rotations, plain coordinates) and keeps the objective, the distance, the weights and the noise.

It ends 250 updates with 4728 and 4847 static scenes in 11 and 12 families (seeds 11 and 12), against 5215 and 5267 in 15 and 17. Missing on both seeds: the spoon inside the upright mug (7 and 2 particles start inside an upright mug, never more than 7 and 8 are there, none after updates 174 and 137, none ever at rest, where the runs above grow the family from 2 and 3 particles to 9 and 22), the spoon leaning on the upright mug, and the tilted-mug families except three scenes. Kept: the spoon inside the mug on its side (57 and 21 static). The two things were changed together, so their separate shares are not measured.

What does not depend on the number of bodies: the objective, the distance, the weights, the noise per body and the cost of an update (one release of the scene per particle). What has no counterpart yet for three bodies or more: the starting law and the relative coordinates. Nothing has been run on more than two bodies.
